_note: Plain-language text for each card: definition, health link, caveat, actions and one source. Sources were checked on 2026-11-14 (see docs/US_DATA_RESEARCH.md); TEAM_CHECK: open every source_url again before the demo and make sure it still works and says what we claim.

hot_days.definition: Days when the temperature reaches 35 °C (95 °F) or more.
hot_days.health_link: People 65 and older, and people with chronic conditions, are more prone to heat-related illness.
hot_days.caveat: NASA POWER averages a ~50 km square, and its daily highs run about 1 °C cooler than weather stations, so a nearby station usually counts more 95 °F days than this card. Trust the trend more than the count.
actions: Choose a home with working air conditioning and a plan for power cuts.
Plan outdoor activity for early morning in the hot season.
Store medicines and inhalers away from heat, as the label says.

warm_nights.definition: Nights when the temperature stays at 24 °C (75 °F) or above.
warm_nights.health_link: Warm nights keep the body from recovering from daytime heat, adding to heat stress the next day.
warm_nights.caveat: This ~50 km average misses a city's extra night-time heat (Phoenix airport's nights run about 3 °C warmer than this grid), so the real city is likely worse than this card.
actions: Keep cooling running overnight during hot spells.
Prefer a bedroom that doesn't face west or sit under the roof.

cold_days.health_link: Long exposure to very cold temperatures can cause hypothermia, which can happen even above 40 °F if a person is wet.
cold_days.caveat: This ~50 km average does not adjust for elevation or cold valleys, so a specific address can see more or fewer very cold nights than shown.
actions: Check the home's insulation and heating costs.
Look for step-free, well-lit entrances that are easy to keep clear of ice.

heavy_rain_days.definition: Days with 20 mm (0.8 in) of rain or more.
heavy_rain_days.health_link: Flooding and water damage can lead to damp and mould at home.
heavy_rain_days.caveat: NASA's model spreads rain over too many days and flattens single-day downpours, so it counts fewer heavy-rain days than a rain gauge. Read the trend, not the number.
heavy_rain_days.source_name: US EPA — A Brief Guide to Mold, Moisture and Your Home
actions: Check the official flood map for the address.
Avoid basement bedrooms; ask about past water damage.
Keep a week of medicines and a go-bag ready in the rainy season.

wettest_day.definition: The most rain that fell in a single day each year.
wettest_day.health_link: The biggest single-day downpours are the ones most likely to cause local flooding.
wettest_day.caveat: NASA's model spreads rain over too many days and flattens single-day downpours, so it counts fewer heavy-rain days than a rain gauge. Read the trend, not the number.

dry_days.definition: Days when average humidity is below 20%.
dry_days.health_link: Very dry air can dry the eyes and skin, and dry, windy days raise wildfire danger.
dry_days.caveat: Humidity here is a ~50 km model average that has not been checked against local stations, so read the trend, not the exact count.
dry_days.source_name: NWS Grand Junction — Fire Weather Criteria
actions: Keep indoor humidity between 30% and 50% with a humidifier.
Clean the humidifier often so it doesn't grow mould.

muggy_days.definition: Days when the dew point is 21 °C (70 °F) or higher — sticky, humid air.
muggy_days.health_link: Long humid spells help mould grow indoors, a common asthma and allergy trigger.
muggy_days.caveat: Dew point is NASA POWER's most station-like value (within about 0.2 °C on average worldwide), but it is still a ~50 km average.
muggy_days.source_name: US EPA — A Brief Guide to Mold, Moisture and Your Home
actions: Keep indoor humidity below 50–60% with air conditioning or a dehumidifier.

pm25.definition: Tiny particles in the air, 2.5 micrometres or smaller, from smoke, traffic, industry and dust.
pm25.health_link: Fine particles can get deep into the lungs, and some into the bloodstream, affecting the lungs and heart and aggravating asthma.
pm25.caveat: NASA's MERRA-2 PM2.5 is a 50 km model estimate without nitrate, so it reads lower than city monitors, especially in winter. Trust the direction of the trend more than the number. It starts in 2010: the model changed how it adds fire smoke that year, and its earlier years read too low where fires matter.
pm25.source_name: US EPA — Health and Environmental Effects of Particulate Matter
actions: Run a HEPA air purifier sized for the bedroom.
Check the daily air quality index; close windows on bad days.

no2.definition: Nitrogen dioxide, a gas mainly from traffic, power plants and industry, measured from space by NASA's OMI instrument.
no2.health_link: NO₂ inflames the airways; longer exposure may contribute to asthma developing.
no2.caveat: Satellite NO2 measures the whole air column above your area, not the air you breathe. It shows whether traffic and industry pollution is rising or falling, and since about 2010 it understates how much street-level NO2 has dropped.
no2.source_name: US EPA — Basic Information about NO2
actions: Prefer homes away from highways and busy junctions.
Keep bedroom windows on the side away from the main road.

fires.definition: Satellite fire detections within 50 km, including farm and prescribed burns.
fires.health_link: Wildfire smoke carries fine particles that worsen asthma, COPD and heart disease, and is a risk in pregnancy.
fires.caveat: Each detection is a 1 km pixel where NASA's MODIS saw a fire at least once. Small, short or cloud-hidden fires are missed and farm and prescribed burns are counted. In oil and gas fields, such as West Texas, many detections are gas flares, not wildfires. So this shows how fire activity nearby changed, not the number of fires or acres burned. Trend from 2003, when the second satellite joined.
fires.source_name: US EPA — Who is at increased risk from wildfire smoke
actions: Have a room you can seal with a HEPA purifier for smoke days.
Sign up for local fire and smoke alerts.

surface_heat.definition: How hot the ground, roofs and roads get on clear summer late mornings, measured by NASA's MODIS satellite at 1 km.
surface_heat.health_link: Neighborhoods with more pavement and fewer trees stay hotter, raising heat stress for people living there.
surface_heat.caveat: MODIS measures how hot the ground and roofs get on a clear summer late morning, which is often much hotter than the air you feel. The trend stops in 2022 because the satellite's orbit drifted, which makes later years read artificially cool.
surface_heat.source_name: US EPA — What Are Heat Islands?
actions: Look for streets with trees and parks nearby.
A light-coloured or well-insulated roof keeps the home cooler.

heat_island.definition: How much hotter the area around the address is than the wider 11 × 11 km area.
heat_island.health_link: Urban heat islands add extra heat on top of the regional climate.
heat_island.caveat: This compares the 3 × 3 km around the address with the 11 × 11 km around it, which is usually also built up, so it is smaller than a city-versus-countryside heat island; in desert cities, irrigated neighborhoods can be cooler than bare ground.
heat_island.source_name: US EPA — What Are Heat Islands?

other_checks.label: Radon (US)
other_checks.text: Radon is a radioactive gas from the ground; the only way to know is to test the home.

other_checks.label: Official flood map (US)
other_checks.text: Check the flood zone for the exact address.

other_checks.label: Local safety statistics
other_checks.text: Check your city or police department's official open data.

humid_heat_days.definition: Days when the air is so hot and humid that sweat stops cooling the body well (daily-mean wet-bulb of 24 °C or more).
humid_heat_days.health_link: Older adults, young children and people with heart disease are most affected by humid heat (CDC).
humid_heat_days.caveat: A ~50 km grid average of the whole day; afternoons are worse, and city streets hold more heat.
actions: Choose a home with working air conditioning and a plan for power cuts.
Plan outdoor activity for early morning in the hot season.

smoke_days.definition: Days with medium or thick wildfire smoke drawn over this place on NOAA's satellite smoke maps.
smoke_days.health_link: Smoke is hardest on people with asthma or COPD, children and older adults (EPA AirNow).
smoke_days.caveat: Counts medium and thick smoke anywhere in the air column, from 2011; on some days it stays high above the ground. Light smoke is left out: it is usually aloft, and NOAA changed how it labels it in 2022. Analysts draw the outlines by hand.
actions: Have a room you can seal with a HEPA purifier for smoke days.
Sign up for local fire and smoke alerts.
smoke_days.actions_source_name: US EPA — Who is at increased risk from wildfire smoke

aod.definition: How hazy the whole column of air is: 0.1 is clear, above 0.4 is hazy (smoke, dust, pollution).
aod.caveat: A model estimate for the whole column of air, not what people breathe at the ground.

rain_sat.definition: All rain and melted snow in a year, measured by a network of satellites.
rain_sat.caveat: Satellite estimates miss some light rain and snow; compare with the NASA POWER rain cards.

surface_heat_5km.definition: How hot the ground gets in the summer sun (June to August, late morning), about 5 km squares.
surface_heat_5km.caveat: Ground temperature, not air temperature. Terra's orbit drift makes 2023–2025 read cool, so the trend stops at 2022.

water_storage.definition: Water stored in the ground, soil and snow, compared with 2004–2009, measured by tiny changes in Earth's gravity.
water_storage.caveat: Regional (about 300 km), so it cannot see one town's wells; there is a gap in mid-2017 to mid-2018.
